newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia to grow at 30-35 percent -- World Bank.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia to grow at 30-35 percent -- World Bank.

text.p: The World Bank said on Thursday it expected Bosnia's economy to grow at a steady rate this year as Serb-controlled territory begins to catch up with the more prosperous Moslem-Croat federation.
The Bosnian economy, fuelled by reconstruction aid, should grow at about 30 to 35 percent in 1997, Rory O'Sullivan, director of the World Bank in Sarajevo, told Reuters.
The country's Moslem-Croat federation is expected to continue to grow at a healthy rate but will fall short of the impressive 50 percent recorded last year, O'Sullivan said.
"We see the overall growth of Bosnia-Herzegovina should be at 30 to 35 percent in 1997 with a slightly slower growth rate in the federation.
"You cannot maintain a 50 percent growth rate, it's just not possible. So we should be coming back to a growth rate of about 20 to 25 percent," he said.
Compared to other countries that endured devastating wars, Bosnia's economy was performing better than some foreign experts had predicted, O'Sullivan said.
A peace treaty which ended the 1992-95 war split Bosnia into two autonomous territories -- the Moslem-Croat federation and the Serb republic.
Official figures estimated GDP in Serb territory at 28 percent last year but foreign experts say the real rate is probably much lower.
The Serb republic's economy has lagged far behind the federation but O'Sullivan said growth was expected to increase if Serb authorities adopt reforms suggested by foreign experts.
The Serb entity has experienced marginal growth partly because reconstruction aid has been tied to compliance with the Dayton peace accords.
Bosnian Serb territory received only about two percent of some $2 billion in aid committed last year because Serb leaders have failed to abide by terms of the Dayton treaty.
O'Sullivan said the Serb entity has also suffered because of its own trade and monetary policies that discourage commerce between the Serb and federation entities and with neighbouring Croatia.
"We are still not at a point where we can say the policies in (the Serb republic) Republika Srpska are the best for stimulating economic growth," he said.
"There are many quantitative restrictions on trade, the level of tariffs in Srpska is much higher than in the federation."

Bosnian Serb territory should benefit from a reform of custom rates agreed by the country's central cabinet last week and the scheduled reopening of border crossings on the northern border with Croatia.
If Serb authorities amend a privatisation law and adopt other measures recommended by foreign experts, then growth could increase significantly in Serb territory, O'Sullivan said.
"Hopefully, with good policies introduced in the next eight weeks or so, we should see a major pick-up in growth in Republika Srpska," he said.
Donor governments are expected to pledge $1.4 billion at a fund-raising conference tentatively scheduled to be held later this month.

With Bosnian Serb leaders still refusing to cooperate with the U.N. war crimes tribunal and other aspects of the peace treaty, O'Sullivan declined to predict how much of that aid donors would decide to award to the Serb entity.
